clue.text: Specialist can stun lot with new presentation

indicators.note: to present something anew is to set the same material out in a fresh arrangement, which is all that happens to these letters

parts.note: ten letters of fodder, three short words straight from the clue

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a sales pitch about dazzling a crowd. Counting those three little words against the enumeration is what gives them away as material rather than description.
explanation.definitionFit: Specialist -> CONSULTANT: in a British hospital the consultant is the most senior specialist doctor, the rank a registrar spends years working towards.

clue.text: Without leader, more silly people lead the way

indicators.note: a word without its leader loses its first letter

parts.note: dafter means sillier
you is used generically for people in general, as in 'you never know'

explanation.surface: Sillier people, with no one in charge, are told to go first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without leader' drops the D from DAFTER. The definition is a whole phrase: 'After you' is the courteous invitation for someone else to go first, that is, lead the way.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'after you' politely invites another person to go ahead first, which is to tell them to lead the way.

clue.text: Faculty with tip for inexperienced Japanese teacher

parts.note: a faculty is a power of perception — sight and hearing are two of the five

indicators.note: the tip of a word written downwards is its topmost letter, so only the opening letter of what follows is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of the word, sitting at the top of a down entry where its tip is

explanation.walkthrough: 'Faculty' looks like a university department, which is exactly what a teacher would belong to. The wordplay wants the older sense, a power of the mind.
explanation.definitionFit: Japanese teacher -> SENSEI: the Japanese form of address for a master or instructor, borrowed into English mostly for martial-arts and karate schools.

clue.text: Two dudes work on radio in foreign capital

indicators.note: something heard on the radio is only heard, so the words are judged by how they sound

parts.note: cat and man are both slang for a dude or guy, and do means work, giving cat man do

explanation.surface: A pair of guys have a job in broadcasting from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: Cat (a hipster) and man are two words for a dude, and do is to work; said together they sound like the name of the city, also spelt Kathmandu.
explanation.definitionFit: Katmandu is the capital city of Nepal, so a capital foreign to the British setter.

clue.text: Tracked vehicles carrying head of Hull's TA

definitions.note: 'Ta' is one informal syllable of gratitude standing in for a noun that is plural in shape; British speech treats the two as exact equivalents.

indicators.note: a vehicle that carries something holds it inside itself rather than towing it along behind

parts.note: tanks run on caterpillar tracks, and these five letters open up after the first

indicators.note: the head of a word is the letter it starts with, and that single letter is all this asks for

parts.note: the front letter of Hull, a port on the Humber in the east of Yorkshire

explanation.walkthrough: TA in the surface is the Territorial Army, which is why the tanks are there. It is really the word you say for a small favour, and the military reading is scenery.
explanation.definitionFit: TA -> THANKS: 'ta' is the everyday British word for thank you, said in a shop or on a bus rather than ever written down.

clue.text: Joint nurse rolled that Keef regularly inhales

indicators.note: to inhale is to take in, so the regular letters of Keef take the reversed nurse inside them
regularly means at regular intervals, so every other letter of Keef is taken

parts.note: the first and third letters of Keef

indicators.note: rolled means turned over, so the nurse word is read backwards

parts.note: EN is the crossword abbreviation for an enrolled nurse

explanation.surface: A nurse rolls a joint that Keith Richards, nicknamed Keef, smokes now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' looks like the cannabis cigarette of the surface but is the body part. 'regularly' takes KE from Keef; 'rolled' turns EN into NE, which KE 'inhales'.
explanation.definitionFit: The knee is the hinge joint between the thigh and the lower leg.

clue.text: Aristocrat's sweet, giving drugs away

indicators.note: giving something away means parting with it, so the drug letters are removed
with giving, away completes the instruction to lose the drug letters

parts.note: a toffee is a chewy sweet
E is the slang abbreviation for the drug ecstasy, so two of them are EE

explanation.surface: A posh person shares a sweet and gives up taking drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'giving drugs away' removes EE (two Es, ecstasy) from TOFFEE. A toff is British slang for an upper-class person.
explanation.definitionFit: A toff is a British informal word for a rich or upper-class person, someone of the gentry.

clue.text: He bargains about carpeting

indicators.note: 'about' in the sense of turned about, facing another way, and letters turned about come out in another order

parts.note: ten letters of fodder, the whole phrase lifted from the clue

explanation.walkthrough: 'Carpeting' is not floor covering: being called onto the carpet in front of the boss is where the word comes from, and the haggling surface hides that entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: carpeting -> EARBASHING: both are informal nouns for a long scolding, one from being summoned onto the carpet, the other from the noise inflicted on your ear.

clue.text: One having frightful ups and downs?

definitions.meaning: the setter means a thing that owns its climbs and plunges literally, being built out of them rather than suffering them
the surface reading is figurative: the reversals of fortune in a bad year, a life lurching from crisis to crisis

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom is figurative — a rollercoaster of a week — and the clue quietly takes it back to the fairground, where the ups and downs are made of steel.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: a fairground ride whose entire existence is steep climbs and terrifying plunges, and nothing in the sentence is wordplay.

clue.text: Tax dope and hash if lacking millions

parts.note: a dope is a fool, an ass

indicators.note: lacking means without, so the millions letter is taken out of the hash word

parts.note: to make a hash of something is to make a mess of it
M is the abbreviation for million or millions

explanation.surface: Drugs, dope and hash, put up for taxation if there is no big money in them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dope' and 'hash' look like drugs but mean a fool and a muddle; 'if lacking' takes the M out of MESS.
explanation.definitionFit: To assess a person or property is to fix the amount of tax they must pay.

clue.text: City folk retired detective deplored

indicators.note: a piece that has retired has gone back the way it came, so its letters read in the opposite order

parts.note: DET is the rank abbreviation on a police detective's name, and it comes in backwards
folk in the old sense is people generally, and here it wants the three-letter word for them
LA is the two-letter short form of Los Angeles

explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired' reads as a pensioned-off policeman and works as an instruction at the same time: one word carrying the surface and the mechanism together.
explanation.definitionFit: deplored -> LAMENTED: both are past-tense verbs for regretting something publicly, a death or a decision, rather than merely disliking it.

clue.text: Quiet period in which set gets a break

indicators.note: what goes in something is buried among its letters, and the phrase names the gap the piece drops into

parts.note: p is the musical mark for piano, the instruction to play softly
a period of history is a time
to set a table is to lay it

explanation.walkthrough: The break wanted is the school one, out in the yard mid-morning, which is about as far from a quiet period in an office as the clue could get.
explanation.definitionFit: a break -> PLAYTIME: the school interval in the middle of the morning, when the class is turned out of the room to run about.

clue.text: Home by latest eleven, primarily to snuggle up

parts.note: a bird's home, built of twigs

indicators.note: what a word is primarily is the letter it opens with, so each of these gives up its first and nothing else

parts.note: the initial letters of the two words, in the order the clue prints them

explanation.walkthrough: An eleven is a cricket or football side, so the surface reads as late team news. That British sports idiom does nothing here except disguise two initials.
explanation.definitionFit: to snuggle up -> NESTLE: to settle yourself into a warm comfortable position against somebody, the verb a cat uses on a lap.

clue.text: We give a hoot if swell lot messes about with it

definitions.note: The setter lets the birds define themselves in the first person, so a plural noun is clued by a sentence they might say rather than by a synonym.

indicators.note: to mess something about is to disturb the arrangement it was in, which is exactly what befalls these letters

parts.note: eight letters of fodder; a swell lot is a fine crowd in the surface
the pronoun joins the mix, two more letters of fodder

explanation.walkthrough: The little owl is a small speckled species brought to Britain in the nineteenth century. 'We give a hoot' has the birds introduce themselves, and caring is not the sense.
explanation.definitionFit: We give a hoot -> LITTLE OWLS: owls hoot, and the idiom for caring is the trap; the adjective picks out one particular small species.

clue.text: Needleworker cut up curtains for alteration

indicators.note: an alteration recuts a garment out of the cloth already there, and the letters are recut the same way

parts.note: thirteen letters of fodder, matching the enumeration exactly

explanation.walkthrough: 'Needleworker' promises a seamstress and 'alteration' a fitting, so the whole sentence points at a sewing room. The needles are the medical kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Needleworker -> ACUPUNCTURIST: someone who treats patients by putting fine needles into them, so the needles are the tools and no sewing is involved.

clue.text: Inappropriate as one going skinny-dipping?

definitions.meaning: the plain sense: not fitting the occasion, the job or the person
somebody swimming naked is wearing no costume, and the word splits into a negative prefix and exactly such a garment

explanation.walkthrough: Eight letters, no wordplay and a question mark to warn you. The joke is that the second reading needs no rearranging at all, only a hyphen you supply yourself.
explanation.definitionFit: Inappropriate -> UNSUITED, not suited to the job or the person; and one going skinny-dipping is literally un-suited, wearing no costume at all.

clue.text: Idleness at work

definitions.note: The second definition fits only once the answer is respaced into two words; as a single word it means the exact opposite of being at work.
definitions.meaning: doing nothing whatever, the state of a machine that has been switched off
busy and operating: the same eight letters with a space dropped into the middle

explanation.walkthrough: Three words and no mechanism, which is why it reads as one phrase. Idleness and industry turn out to be the same spelling with the gap in a different place.
explanation.definitionFit: Idleness -> INACTION, doing nothing at all; and 'at work' -> IN ACTION, the same letters respaced into a phrase meaning busy.

clue.text: Beastly types love to interfere with data

indicators.note: to interfere with something is to get into it and meddle, so the letter lands inside rather than alongside

parts.note: stats are the figures a data set boils down to, and they open up after the second letter
love is a score of nothing at tennis, written as the round O

explanation.walkthrough: 'Beastly' reads as an adjective of complaint, a beastly cold day, and is really pointing at animals: small vicious ones out of the weasel family.
explanation.definitionFit: Beastly types -> STOATS: definition by example, a beast being any animal, and these are the slim brown hunters that turn white in winter.

clue.text: Turn on a banker that's embezzled Rand

indicators.note: to embezzle is to take money quietly into your own keeping, so the letter named is tucked away inside

parts.note: the article is taken at face value, one letter straight from the clue
a banker in crosswords is a river, because a river is the thing with banks; the Ouse flows through York
R is the letter on a South African price tag, the rand being the currency there

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a fraud story from first word to last, and the only banker in the parse is a stretch of water. That pun is a setter's standby worth learning early.
explanation.definitionFit: Turn on -> AROUSE: to excite or awaken somebody, with 'turn on' the everyday phrase for producing that same effect.

clue.text: Truly pretend to be posh to get partner

parts.note: somebody pretending to feel something is putting on an act
U is the crossword letter for upper class, from the old British talk of U and non-U speech
an ally is a partner in a war or a deal

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a social climber putting on a voice. The definition is the single word at the front, which is easy to miss because it reads as part of the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Truly -> ACTUALLY, since both adverbs insist that what follows is the case, though the longer one often carries a hint of correcting somebody.

clue.text: Quality wood needing to be delivered

indicators.note: a speech or a line is delivered out loud, so what counts is the sound of the word and not its spelling

parts.note: the wood a builder orders by the yard is timber, and spoken aloud that word can be written a second way

explanation.walkthrough: 'Quality wood' sits together so comfortably that the definition looks like both words. Only the first is it, and the second is there to be heard rather than read.
explanation.definitionFit: Quality -> TIMBRE: the quality of a sound that lets you tell a violin from a flute playing the very same note.

clue.text: Job in bank filled by academic playboy?

indicators.note: a space filled by something has that thing put within it, so the shorter piece goes inside the longer

parts.note: a bank job is a heist, five letters that split after the second
a don is a senior member of an Oxford or Cambridge college

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is doing real work. A playboy is not the definition so much as one specimen of it, and the robbery in the surface never happens.
explanation.definitionFit: playboy? -> HEDONIST: definition by example — a playboy is one kind of pleasure-seeker, and the question mark admits the wider word is wanted.

clue.text: Men in extremes of strife flipping love God

indicators.note: flipping means turning over, so the whole construction is read backwards
in places the men letters between the outer letters of strife
the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of strife
OR, other ranks, is the military abbreviation for soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: Soldiers caught up in conflict curse the god of love in exasperation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremes of' strife gives SE; 'in' puts OR inside to make SORE, and 'flipping' turns that round. Flipping also pretends to be a mild British oath in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Eros is the Greek god of desire and love, the counterpart of the Roman Cupid.

clue.text: Medium-size, unopened concoction for evacuation

parts.note: M is the clothing-size abbreviation for medium

indicators.note: unopened means without its opening, so the first letter of the concoction word goes

parts.note: a potion is a mixed drink or concoction

explanation.surface: A medium-sized bottle of potion, still sealed, is kept for an emergency evacuation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unopened' drops the P of POTION. Evacuation here is not leaving a building but emptying the bowels.
explanation.definitionFit: A motion is a bowel movement, the act of emptying the bowels, which is the medical sense of evacuation.

clue.text: One who perjures or frees war criminal

indicators.note: a criminal is somebody bent out of true, and letters described that way come out bent out of their order

parts.note: ten letters of fodder, the three words sitting between definition and indicator

explanation.walkthrough: 'War criminal' is one phrase in the surface and two separate jobs in the parse: the last word is the instruction, not part of the picture it paints.
explanation.definitionFit: One who perjures -> FORSWEARER: to forswear is to swear falsely or renounce upon oath, so the noun names whoever does it.

clue.text: Go slowly … jams in capital city abroad

indicators.note: to jam something in is to force it into a space it barely fits, which is how tightly these letters are packed

parts.note: four consecutive letters, the run starting at the end of the first word and carrying on into the next

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis and the traffic make it look like a sentence about a jam. The letters have been sitting in plain sight since the first two words of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: capital city abroad -> OSLO: Norway's capital, at the head of a long fjord, and abroad from the London paper this puzzle appears in.
